slides.myth: A wall of flames is what takes homes in a wildfire
slides.truth: Most homes lost aren't touched by flames. Wind-blown embers do it.
slides.body: Embers land well ahead of the fire — in gutters, vents, and roof debris. And the biggest ember target on your property is the roof.

caption:
This is the fact that changed how we think about our own houses: most homes lost to wildfire are never reached by the flame front. They're lit by embers riding the wind, sometimes from a fire that's still miles out.

Which means wildfire defense isn't mostly about heroics — it's about a roof and gutters that give embers nothing to work with. That's a maintenance problem, and maintenance problems are solvable.

Tomorrow we'll walk through exactly how embers get in. Want your roof and vents looked at first? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: How embers actually get into a house
Gutters packed with fir needles
slides.body: The classic Douglas County failure: an ember lands in dry needles, ignites, and the fire climbs into the roof edge. Clean gutters — or guards — close this door.

slides.headline: Open attic and soffit vents
slides.body: Vents inhale embers straight into the driest space in the house. Fine 1/8" metal mesh blocks them while keeping the airflow your attic needs.

slides.headline: Needle drifts on the roof itself
slides.body: Valleys and the spots behind chimneys collect ember fuel that sits right on top of your fire-rated roof. Seasonal clearing matters as much as the material.

slides.headline: Half of ember defense is maintenance
slides.body: A Class A roof buried in dry needles has given back much of its advantage. Keep the doors shut and the rating actually means something.

caption:
Embers are small, wind-driven, and patient. They don't defeat a modern roof covering very often — they find the gaps around it.

The three usual entry points: gutters full of dry fir needles, unscreened attic vents, and debris drifts sitting in the valleys. All three are fixable, and none of them require a new roof.

If you're up a timbered draw or anywhere near the county's fire country, an hour of honest maintenance before August is worth more than any product brochure. We can handle it if ladders aren't your thing — call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: What does "Class A" actually mean?
The top fire rating a roof can earn
slides.body: Roofs are rated Class A, B, or C in standardized burn tests. Class A means the assembly resists severe fire exposure — including burning brands sitting on the surface.

slides.headline: "Assembly" is the key word
slides.body: The rating belongs to covering PLUS underlayment — not the top layer alone. This is that underlayment on one of our metal jobs. Ask which rated assembly you're getting.

slides.headline: How Douglas County roofs get to Class A
slides.body: If your comp roof is reasonably modern, you may already have one.

caption:
"Class A" gets thrown around like a brand name, so here's the plain version: it's the top fire rating a roof assembly can earn, tested with burning material sitting directly on the surface.

The catch most people miss is the word assembly. The rating belongs to the whole system — covering plus underlayment — not the shingle or panel alone. A great product over the wrong underlayment may not make the rating. It's exactly the kind of detail a written bid should spell out.

slides.myth: Metal roofs are loud when it rains
slides.truth: On a house, rain lands within a few decibels of asphalt.
slides.body: The drumming you remember was a barn — bare metal over open framing. A home adds solid decking, underlayment, and an insulated attic that soak up the sound.

caption:
The number one question we get about metal roofing: "won't it be loud when it rains?" Fair worry — everyone's stood under a carport in a downpour.

But that's bare metal over open framing, where the panel IS the ceiling. A residential metal roof goes over solid sheathing and underlayment, above an insulated attic. All that mass absorbs the sound, and most homeowners honestly can't tell the difference from the living room.

In a place with 130 rain days a year, if metal roofs were loud, western Oregon would have noticed by now. Questions? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Years a well-installed metal roof lasts here
slides.body: Asphalt manages about 20–25 in our wet-dry climate — less if moss goes unmanaged. Metal roughly doubles or triples it, and sheds the moss and needles along the way.

caption:
40 to 70 years. That's the honest range for well-installed residential metal in our climate — against roughly 20–25 for architectural asphalt, and less than that if moss gets a foothold.

Put differently: a metal roof installed today plausibly outlasts the mortgage, the truck, and a few appliances' worth of everything else. It's most of the answer to why people pay more upfront for it.

slides.headline: Metal vs. asphalt, from a crew that installs both
Asphalt wins the day you pay
slides.body: Most Douglas County asphalt replacements land roughly $10,000–$25,000. Metal runs about 2–3x that for the same roof. No way around it.

slides.headline: Rain days a year — and moss loves asphalt
slides.body: Granular shingles give moss a perfect anchor. Smooth metal gives it nothing to grip, and fir needles slide off instead of composting. The big local advantage.

slides.headline: 20–25 years vs. 40–70
slides.body: Per year of service they're nearly the same roof. The real difference is when you pay: asphalt spreads it across two or three replacements; metal front-loads it once.

caption:
Ask three roofers "metal or asphalt?" and you'll usually learn more about what they sell than what you need. We install both in roughly equal seriousness, so our only stake is you not regretting the choice in ten years.

Short version: both are good roofs, good at different things. Metal solves moss with money; asphalt solves it with maintenance. Metal front-loads the cost once; asphalt spreads it across replacements.

slides.headline: Sometimes asphalt is simply the right answer
slides.body: A quality Class A architectural asphalt roof is a genuinely good roof — not a consolation prize.

caption:
Metal evangelists skip this part. We won't.

If $15,000 is what the project can bear, a well-executed architectural asphalt roof — Class A, algae-resistant, properly flashed — beats a stretched-budget metal job that shortchanges the details. Lots of valleys and dormers multiply metal's cost. On some streets a metal roof is a statement you didn't mean to make. And if you're selling in five years, you'd pay metal's full premium and hand the lifespan to the next owner.

slides.myth: Every roof in the Umpqua Valley grows moss eventually
slides.truth: Metal's smooth surface gives moss rhizoids nothing to grip.
slides.body: Fir needles slide off instead of composting in the valleys. Choosing metal deletes a maintenance line item asphalt owners here carry for the life of the roof.

caption:
We live in world-class moss habitat — it's the number one killer of asphalt roofs in this valley. But moss needs something to hold onto, and a painted metal panel offers it nothing. No granular texture for rhizoids to anchor in, no needle compost building up in the valleys.

That's metal's quietest superpower here. Not the look, not even the fire rating — the fact that the $250–$600 professional moss treatment cycle simply stops applying to your house.

slides.headline: Standing seam vs. corrugated: the two metal roofs
Hidden clips, no holes in the weather surface
slides.body: Panels lock together at raised seams and float on concealed clips as temperatures swing. No fastener ever pierces what the rain touches. The premium system.

slides.headline: Thousands of gasketed screws — and that's fine
slides.body: Screwed straight through the panel face, each sealed by a rubber washer. Simpler, faster, the least expensive metal. That's its whole argument, and it's a good one.

slides.headline: Match the system to the building
bullets: Standing seam → the house you live in
Both shed moss and rate Class A

caption:
"Metal roof" covers two very different products — one held on by hidden clips, one by thousands of rubber-gasketed screws. The difference is exactly where it matters most in a climate with 130 rainy days: how the panel is attached.

Our plain recommendation for rural Douglas County places: screw-down on the outbuildings, standing seam on the house. A shop is the perfect home for corrugated — low stakes per leak, budget better spent on what's inside. The house is where concealed fasteners earn their premium.

House, shop, or both — call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Years in, every screw-down roof wants a fastener check
slides.body: Rubber gaskets harden in our soak-then-bake cycle while the panels work screws loose. Re-drive, re-gasket, repeat. Routine — not a defect.

caption:
If you own a screw-down metal roof — house, shop, or barn — put this on the long-term calendar: a fastener inspection around years 10–15, and periodically after.

Every gasketed screw is a small rubber part doing a big job, and Douglas County's soaked-October-to-May, baked-all-summer cycle ages them while the steel expands and contracts around the shanks. Skip the check and each tired gasket becomes a slow pinhole leak that shows up as a rust streak or a drip on the tractor.

slides.headline: Wildfire ash on your roof: the cleanup nobody explains
Abrasive when dry, caustic when wet
slides.body: Hard, gritty particles sand the granules off shingles if scrubbed. Add water and ash turns into an alkaline sludge that's hard on gutters and metal finishes.

slides.myth: A pressure washer is the fast way to clean ash off
slides.truth: Blasting strips granules and drives ash slurry under the shingles.

slides.headline: Gentle is the entire game
bullets: N95 on, wait for calm air
Soft brush or low leaf blower
Hose rinse, ridge down, low pressure
Flush gutters before the first rain

caption:
Every smoke season leaves a gray film on Douglas County roofs, and almost nobody talks about what it does up there — or how easy it is to make it worse.

Left alone, a light dusting mostly rinses away with the first rains. The real damage comes from heavy ash concentrating in gutters, and from well-meaning cleanup done wrong: dry-scrubbing grinds abrasive ash into the granules, and pressure washing does everything wrong at once.

Steep roof, heavy ash, or just done with ladder-work in a mask? We do ash-season flushes every fall. Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Flush gutters after smoke season — before the first real rain
slides.body: Dry ash rinses out of a gutter easily. Wait for the October storms and it mixes with needles into gray cement that packs your downspouts right as the wet season starts.

caption:
Here's the sequence that plays out across the valley every fall: ash collects in gutters through August and September, mixing with fir needles. Then the first storms turn that dry mix into dense, concrete-like sludge that clogs downspouts at the exact moment seven months of rain begin.

The whole fix is timing. A hose flush in late September or early October takes minutes. The November version has to be dug out by hand, one scoop at a time.

slides.headline: Since 2020, insurers grade Douglas County roofs
slides.body: A Class A roof can earn discounts — or be the thing that keeps you insurable. Save the invoice naming the product, the permit, and photos, and send copies to your agent.

caption:
Since the 2020 fires, wildfire has reshaped Oregon homeowners insurance, and Douglas County homeowners are seeing both ends of it. Carrots: some insurers offer discounts or preferred rates for Class A roofs and documented home-hardening. Sticks: in higher-risk areas, carriers increasingly ask about roof material and age at renewal — and nonrenewal pressure is real for old shake roofs and visibly deferred maintenance.

The homeowners who benefit are the ones who can prove it. Every replacement we do comes with that paperwork — product line, permit record, photos. Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Lean, clean, green — what the roof needs from the yard
Keep the ring around the house bare of fuel
slides.body: No bark mulch, dry plants, or stacked firewood against the walls. Embers that land here have nothing to start with.

slides.headline: Don't let branches overhang the roof
slides.body: They drop the very needle litter embers ignite — and feed the moss problem the rest of the year. Trimming pays twice.

slides.headline: We're roofers, not a wildland crew
slides.body: The roof works with the ground around it. OSU Extension and your local fire district publish full defensible-space guides — genuinely worth an evening.

caption:
Defensible space isn't our trade, so we'll keep to the parts that meet the roof: keep the first five feet around the house free of bark mulch, dry plants, and stacked firewood; limb up trees near the structure; and don't let branches overhang the roofline.

That last one is the twofer. Overhanging limbs drop the needle litter that embers ignite in August — and feed the moss that eats shingles from October to May. One afternoon with a pole saw works both seasons.

Want the roof-and-gutter half assessed honestly? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: A gutter full of dry fir needles is a fuse on your roof edge
slides.body: The classic failure: an ember lands in packed needles, ignites, and climbs into the roofline. Clean gutters — or guards that keep needles out — close that door.

caption:
Of all the ember entry points on a Douglas County house, this is the one we'd fix first — because it's the cheapest and the most common.

An ember doesn't need to defeat your roof covering. It just needs to land in a gutter packed with a summer's worth of dry fir needles, sitting inches from the roof edge. Regular cleaning closes that door; gutter guards keep it closed without the ladder trips.
